```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.align = "center"
)
```

## Data and libraries

We use the `instacart` data from `p8105.datasets`, along with `tidyverse` and
`plotly`.

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(plotly)

data("instacart")
```

The full dataset has over 1.3 million rows. That is fine for plots that
aggregate first, but slow for one that draws a point or a box per observation,
so we also take a random sample of 50,000 rows. The seed makes that sample
reproducible.

```{r sample}
set.seed(123)

instacart_sample =
  instacart |>
  slice_sample(n = 50000)
```

## Plotly

### Scatterplot

Instacart has no two continuous variables measured on the same row, so a
scatterplot needs an aggregation step first. Summarising to one row per aisle
gives us order volume and reorder rate as a pair, and we keep aisles with more
than 1,000 items. Volume spans several orders of magnitude, so the x-axis is
log-scaled, and `text` with `hoverinfo = "text"` replaces the default hover
box with a labelled one.

```{r scatterplot}
instacart |>
  group_by(department, aisle) |>
  summarize(
    n_items = n(),
    reorder_rate = mean(reordered),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_items > 1000) |>
  mutate(
    text_label =
      str_c("Aisle: ", aisle,
            "\nDepartment: ", department,
            "\nItems: ", n_items,
            "\nReorder rate: ", round(reorder_rate, 3))) |>
  plot_ly(
    x = ~n_items,
    y = ~reorder_rate,
    color = ~department,
    text = ~text_label,
    hoverinfo = "text",
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "markers",
    marker = list(size = 9, opacity = 0.7),
    colors = "viridis") |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "Number of items ordered", type = "log"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Proportion of items reordered"),
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Department")))
```

### Histogram

The distribution of days since the prior order, across all orders with a
value. One bin per day gives 31 bins, and `bargap` adds a little space between
them. Note the spike in the final bin: Instacart caps this variable at 30
days, so that bar collects every longer gap as well.

```{r histogram}
instacart |>
  filter(!is.na(days_since_prior_order)) |>
  plot_ly(
    x = ~days_since_prior_order,
    type = "histogram",
    nbinsx = 31,
    marker = list(color = "#21908CFF")) |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "Days since prior order"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Number of items ordered"),
    bargap = 0.05)
```

### Boxplots

Hour of day by department, using the 50,000-row sample. Departments are
reordered by median hour with `fct_reorder`, which makes the ordering
meaningful rather than alphabetical, and the legend is switched off because
the x-axis already labels each box.

```{r boxplots}
instacart_sample |>
  mutate(
    department = fct_reorder(
      department, order_hour_of_day)) |>
  plot_ly(
    x = ~department,
    y = ~order_hour_of_day,
    color = ~department,
    type = "box",
    colors = "viridis") |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "Department"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Hour of day"),
    showlegend = FALSE)
```

### ggplotly

The same aisle-level scatterplot, built in `ggplot2` and then made interactive
with `ggplotly()`. Hover text comes from the `text` aesthetic, which `ggplot2`
ignores when drawing and `ggplotly()` picks up.

```{r ggplotly}
aisle_plot =
  instacart |>
  group_by(department, aisle) |>
  summarize(
    n_items = n(),
    reorder_rate = mean(reordered),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_items > 1000) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_items, y = reorder_rate, color = department, text = aisle)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  viridis::scale_color_viridis(discrete = TRUE) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of items ordered",
    y = "Proportion of items reordered",
    color = "Department")

ggplotly(aisle_plot)
```
